questions.text: For the formation of a solution, the total free-energy change is given by:
questions.detailed: Mixing is governed by $\Delta G_{\text{mix}}=\Delta H_{\text{mix}}-T\Delta S_{\text{mix}}$. Whether a solution forms depends on the tug-of-war between the enthalpy of mixing and the entropy of mixing — the heart of this whole topic.

questions.text: For an *ideal* solution, which statement is true?

options.label: a
options.text: $\Delta H_{\text{mix}}=0$ and $\Delta S_{\text{mix}}$ is the ideal configurational value

questions.detailed: An ideal solution has no enthalpy of mixing ($\Delta H_{\text{mix}}=0$, meaning A–A, B–B and A–B interactions are energetically identical), and the entropy of mixing is the purely statistical $\Delta S_{\text{mix}}=-R\sum_i x_i\ln x_i$.

questions.text: The ideal entropy of mixing for an equimolar binary solution is (per mole, $R=8.314$):
questions.detailed: $\Delta S_{\text{mix}}=-R(x_A\ln x_A+x_B\ln x_B)=-R(0.5\ln0.5+0.5\ln0.5)=R\ln2=8.314\times0.693=+5.76\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$ per mole. Mixing always raises entropy, so this is positive.

questions.text: The ideal free energy of mixing as a function of composition is:
questions.detailed: With $\Delta H_{\text{mix}}=0$, $\Delta G_{\text{mix}}=-T\Delta S_{\text{mix}}=RT\sum_i x_i\ln x_i$. Since each $\ln x_i<0$, $\Delta G_{\text{mix}}<0$ everywhere — an ideal solution is always stable and never demixes.

questions.text: In the regular solution model, the enthalpy of mixing is written as:
questions.detailed: A regular solution keeps the ideal entropy of mixing but adds an enthalpy term $\Delta H_{\text{mix}}=\Omega x_A x_B$ (with $\Omega$ the interaction parameter, roughly $N z[\varepsilon_{AB}-\tfrac12(\varepsilon_{AA}+\varepsilon_{BB})]$). The $x_A x_B$ factor peaks at $x=0.5$.

questions.text: A positive interaction parameter $\Omega>0$ in the regular model implies:

options.label: a
options.text: A–B bonds are weaker than the average of A–A and B–B, so the system tends to unmix

questions.detailed: $\Omega>0$ means like atoms prefer each other ($\varepsilon_{AB}$ less favourable), giving a positive $\Delta H_{\text{mix}}$, positive deviation from Raoult's law, and a tendency toward a miscibility gap at low temperature. $\Omega<0$ promotes ordering/compound formation.

questions.text: For a symmetric regular solution, the critical value of $\Omega$ above which a miscibility gap appears is:
questions.detailed: Demixing occurs when the interaction parameter exceeds $\Omega_c=2RT$ (for a symmetric regular solution). Equivalently, below the critical temperature $T_c=\Omega/(2R)$ the single-phase solution becomes unstable over a composition range.

questions.text: A regular solution has $\Omega=20\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$. Its critical (consolute) temperature for demixing is about:
questions.detailed: $T_c=\Omega/(2R)=20{,}000/(2\times8.314)\approx1203\ \mathrm{K}$. Below $T_c$ the alloy separates into two phases; above it, it is a single homogeneous solution.

questions.text: The excess Gibbs energy of a regular solution is:
questions.detailed: A regular solution is defined by $S^{E}=0$ (ideal entropy) and $H^{E}=\Omega x_A x_B$. Hence $G^{E}=H^{E}-TS^{E}=\Omega x_A x_B$. The excess functions measure deviation from ideal behaviour.

questions.text: For a regular solution, the activity coefficient of component A is related to $\Omega$ by:
questions.detailed: Integrating the Gibbs–Duhem relation for the regular model gives $RT\ln\gamma_A=\Omega x_B^2$ and $RT\ln\gamma_B=\Omega x_A^2$. So $\gamma>1$ when $\Omega>0$ (positive deviation), $\gamma<1$ when $\Omega<0$.

questions.text: The *binodal* (coexistence) curve on a free-energy diagram is found by:

options.label: a
options.text: Drawing the common tangent to the two free-energy minima and reading its points of contact

questions.detailed: The binodal (equilibrium phase boundary) is the locus of points where a single common tangent touches the $G$–$x$ curve, because equality of chemical potentials in both phases is exactly the common-tangent condition. The points of tangency give the two coexisting compositions.

questions.text: The *spinodal* curve is defined by the condition:
questions.detailed: The spinodal is the locus of inflection points where $\partial^2G/\partial x^2=0$. Inside it $\partial^2G/\partial x^2<0$ — the solution is *unstable* to infinitesimal composition fluctuations. Outside it but inside the binodal, the solution is merely metastable (needs nucleation).

questions.text: Which statement about the spinodal and binodal is correct?

options.label: a
options.text: The spinodal lies inside the binodal; the two curves touch at the critical point

options.label: b
options.text: The spinodal lies outside the binodal

options.label: d
options.text: The binodal lies inside the spinodal

questions.detailed: The spinodal (limit of instability) is nested inside the binodal (limit of metastability). Between the two curves the phase is metastable; inside the spinodal it is unstable and decomposes spontaneously with no nucleation barrier.

questions.text: For a symmetric regular solution the spinodal boundaries at a given $T$ satisfy $RT=2\Omega\,x(1-x)$. At the critical point this gives $x=$:
questions.detailed: Susceptibility $\partial^2G/\partial x^2=0$ requires $RT=2\Omega x(1-x)$. The maximum of $x(1-x)$ is at $x=0.5$, which sets the critical composition; there $RT_c=2\Omega(0.25)=\Omega/2$, i.e. $T_c=\Omega/2R$.

questions.text: The sub-regular solution model differs from the regular model in that:

options.label: a
options.text: The interaction parameter $\Omega$ itself varies with composition

options.label: b
options.text: The entropy of mixing is zero

options.label: c
options.text: There is no enthalpy of mixing

questions.detailed: A sub-regular solution allows $\Omega$ to depend on composition (e.g. $\Omega=A x_A+B x_B$, or a polynomial in $x$), which better reproduces asymmetric real systems and asymmetric miscibility gaps.

questions.text: The Flory–Huggins model extends the regular-solution theory mainly to account for:

options.label: a
options.text: The large size difference between polymer molecules, using volume fractions and an entropy term corrected for chain length

questions.detailed: In polymer blends the species differ greatly in molar volume, so the simple $x\ln x$ entropy no longer applies. Flory–Huggins uses volume fractions $\phi$ and a size ratio, plus an interaction parameter $\chi$, to describe polymer mixing quantitatively.

questions.text: In the Flory–Huggins model, the interaction parameter is usually denoted:
questions.detailed: Flory–Huggins uses $\chi$ (chi), the per-lattice-site interaction parameter, feeding into $\Delta G_{\text{mix}}$ together with the combinatorial entropy term in volume fractions. It is conceptually the polymer analogue of $\Omega/RT$.

questions.text: A regular solution has $\Omega=20\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ at $T=1000\ \mathrm{K}$. The ratio $\Omega/RT$ is about:
questions.detailed: $RT=8.314\times1000=8314\ \mathrm{J}$; $\Omega/RT=20{,}000/8314\approx2.4$. Since this exceeds the critical value of $2$, the solution has a miscibility gap at 1000 K for a symmetric regular model.

questions.text: Which statements about the ideal entropy of mixing are correct?

statements.text: It is always positive for mixing two species.
It is maximum at equimolar composition.

questions.detailed: $\Delta S_{\text{mix}}=-R\sum x_i\ln x_i$ is positive (I) and largest at $x=0.5$ (II). It contains no temperature dependence (III is false) — the entropy of mixing is purely configurational.

questions.text: Inside the spinodal region, a composition fluctuation will:

options.label: a
options.text: Decay back to the homogeneous state

options.label: b
options.text: Grow spontaneously because the free energy decreases, leading to spinodal decomposition

questions.detailed: When $\partial^2G/\partial x^2<0$ (inside the spinodal), any small composition wave *lowers* $G$, so it grows spontaneously — uphill diffusion, the signature of spinodal decomposition, with no nucleation barrier.

questions.text: Which of the following produces an *asymmetric* miscibility gap?

options.label: b
options.text: A sub-regular solution with a composition-dependent $\Omega$

questions.detailed: A composition-dependent interaction parameter ($\Omega=\Omega_1 x_A+\Omega_2 x_B$) makes the $G$–$x$ curve asymmetric, so the common-tangent construction yields an asymmetric gap — typical of real alloy systems.

questions.text: For a regular solution with $\Omega=6{,}000\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$ at $T=500\ \mathrm{K}$, is a single-phase solution stable?
questions.detailed: $RT=8.314\times500=4157$, so $\Omega/RT=6000/4157\approx1.44$, which is *less* than 2. The single-phase solution is therefore stable. Demixing would require $\Omega/RT>2$.

questions.text: Which statement about excess functions is correct?
questions.detailed: The excess Gibbs energy is $G^{E}=G_{\text{real}}-G_{\text{ideal}}=RT\sum_i x_i\ln\gamma_i$. It vanishes for an ideal solution ($\gamma_i=1$) and quantifies the departure from ideality driven by non-zero $H^{E}$ and $S^{E}$.

questions.text: Choose the correct option:
questions.assertion: An ideal solution never separates into two phases at any temperature.
questions.reason: For an ideal solution the free energy of mixing is negative at every composition.

options.label: a
options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

options.label: b
options.text: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

options.label: c
options.text: A is true but R is false

options.label: d
options.text: A is false but R is true

questions.detailed: For an ideal solution $\Delta G_{\text{mix}}=RT\sum x_i\ln x_i<0$ and the $G$–$x$ curve is convex everywhere, so no common tangent to two separate minima can be drawn — no demixing. R (always-negative $\Delta G_{\text{mix}}$) is exactly why A holds.

questions.text: The common-tangent construction on a molar free-energy diagram gives directly:

options.label: a
options.text: The compositions of the two coexisting phases at equilibrium

questions.detailed: The common tangent touches the $G$–$x$ curve at the two equilibrium phase compositions; these are the binodal points. The tangent's intercepts also give the chemical potentials $\mu_A$ and $\mu_B$.

questions.text: For a symmetric regular solution the critical composition and critical temperature are:
questions.detailed: Both spinodal and binodal meet at $x_c=0.5$, where $T_c=\Omega/2R$. This single point is the consolute (critical solution) point; below $T_c$ a miscibility gap opens.

questions.text: "A negative value of $\Omega$ leads to a tendency for ordering or compound formation rather than demixing."
questions.detailed: True. $\Omega<0$ means unlike atoms attract each other more strongly than like atoms, giving $\Delta H_{\text{mix}}<0$, negative deviation from Raoult's law, and short-range ordering or intermetallic compound formation.
